Hypoxemia

five mechanisms · A-a gradient · response to oxygen · shunt vs ventilation-perfusion mismatch · saturation gapIs the A-a gradient widened, and does the hypoxemia correct when inspired oxygen rises?

1Presentation2Urgent3Differential4Workup5Criteria6Severity7Treatment8Follow-upPractice
1Presentation
Bottom line
  • Low saturation an arterial blood gas first: a normal PaO2 (arterial oxygen pressure) means the hemoglobin is the problem (methemoglobin, carbon monoxide)
  • Low PaO2 the A-a (alveolar-arterial) gradient: normal means hypoventilation or low inspired oxygen; widened means V/Q (ventilation-perfusion) mismatch, shunt or a diffusion defect
  • Widened and corrects on oxygen V/Q mismatch; stays low shunt: recruit the alveoli (CPAP, continuous positive airway pressure; PEEP; surfactant) rather than turning the oxygen up
What it is

Low arterial oxygen; the mechanism is named before the disease

Sort by

PaO2 low or only the reading Normal valueAlveolar minus arterial oxygen pressure; normal is approximately (age/4) + 4 the response to oxygen

Hands off

Surfactant deficiency: Lung Disease in the Newborn and Preterm Infant; cyanosis at rest in a newborn: Cyanosis in the Newborn; oxygen in carbon dioxide retainers: COPD; embolism: Venous Thromboembolism

2Urgent risks
ShuntSaturation stays below 90% on supplemental oxygen
More oxygen will not fix it

If alveoli are collapsed or flooded, choose recruit them: CPAP or PEEP (positive end-expiratory pressure), surfactant in the preterm newborn.

Carbon monoxideHeadache and nausea in people sharing a heated home (furnace, gas heater); a normal pulse oximeter reading

If exposure is possible, choose co-oximetry, and 100% oxygen by nonrebreather mask without waiting.

HypoventilationSlow breathing, pinpoint pupils, PaCO2 ↑

If opioid overdose is suspected, choose naloxone, a diagnostic and therapeutic step.

Carbon dioxide retentionCOPD (chronic obstructive pulmonary disease) on supplemental oxygen
Oxygen can raise dead space and the PaCO2

If a carbon dioxide retainer needs oxygen, choose titrate to a saturation of 88 to 92%, not higher.

3Differential
Mechanisms, most tempting first
MechanismClueDecides it
Intrapulmonary shunt (V/Q = 0)Perfused but unventilated alveoli: respiratory distress syndrome, collapse, pneumonia, ARDS (acute respiratory distress syndrome), edemaWidened gradient; little rise even on 100% oxygen; corrected by recruitment
V/Q mismatchAsthma, COPD, early pneumonia; the commonest mechanism in adultsWidened gradient that corrects on a few liters of oxygen
Shunt with clear lungsCyanotic heart disease, hepatopulmonary syndrome, a patent foramen ovale opened by right-sided pressure; clear lungsNo rise in PaO2 on 100% oxygen with clear lungs
Sudden dyspnea, clear chestHyperventilation, PaCO2 ↓, respiratory alkalosis
HypoventilationOpioids, neuromuscular disease, obesity hypoventilationNormal gradient, PaCO2 ↑
Low inspired oxygenAltitudeNormal gradient, PaCO2 ↓ from hyperventilation
Diffusion defectInterstitial disease or emphysema; often normal at restDesaturates only on exertion; low DLCO (diffusing capacity for carbon monoxide)
Hemoglobin problemCarbon monoxide, methemoglobin; cyanosis unmoved by oxygenNormal PaO2 with a low or falsely normal reading
4Workup
Clues that change the answer
CluePoints toNext move
Preterm, grunting, decreased breath sounds on both sides at 1 hour; still low on CPAP (continuous positive airway pressure) with 30% oxygenIntrapulmonary shunt from surfactant deficiency, not apnea of prematurity (that comes days later, without effort)Surfactant and CPAP, not more oxygen
Chocolate-colored blood; a reading of about 85% that often stays low on oxygen; after benzocaineMethemoglobinemiaMethylene blue
Newborn cyanotic at rest, clear lungs, no rise on 100% oxygenCyanotic heart diseaseEchocardiogram
Left-to-right shunt offered as the causeCannot desaturate: it recirculates oxygenated bloodLook for another mechanism
Pause point
The FiO2 (inspired oxygen fraction) rises and the saturation does not follow Offered: turning the oxygen up A shunt → Stop titrating and recruit the alveoli

In carbon monoxide poisoning a normal pulse oximeter reading is falsely reassuring.

Practice
  1. 27 wk preterm M, 3 h old, grunting, ground-glass film with air bronchograms, SpO2 85% on CPAP FiO2 0.6 and rising → Intubate and give intratracheal surfactant → Neonatal respiratory distress syndrome
  2. 24 yo M, postoperative day (POD) 1, RR 6, pinpoint pupils, PaO2 55, PaCO2 68, normal A-a gradient → Naloxone → Opioid-induced hypoventilation
  3. 4 mo F, cyanosis after topical teething gel, chocolate-brown blood, SpO2 fixed at 85% on 100% oxygen, PaO2 96 → Methylene blue IV → Methemoglobinemia
  4. 34 yo F and two housemates with headache and nausea after a furnace failure, COHb (carboxyhemoglobin) 18%, no syncope, normal neurologic exam → High-flow 100% oxygen by nonrebreather → Carbon monoxide poisoning
  5. 58 yo M with ARDS, PaO2 58 on FiO2 0.8 with PEEP 8, diffuse bilateral opacities → Increase PEEP → Refractory intrapulmonary shunt
  6. 68 yo M, COPD exacerbation, baseline PaCO2 62, now receiving oxygen → Titrating oxygen to a saturation of 100% → Oxygen-induced hypercapnia
  7. 62 yo F, 8 months of exertional dyspnea, resting SpO2 96% falling to 86% with ambulation, clear lungs, normal chest film → Diffusing capacity for carbon monoxide → Diffusion limitation
  8. 44 yo F, POD 5 from knee arthroplasty, sudden dyspnea, clear lungs, normal film, widened A-a gradient → CT pulmonary angiography → Pulmonary embolism
  9. 29 yo M trekker at 4,500 m, dyspnea with SpO2 84%, clear lungs, PaCO2 30, normal A-a gradient → Reduced inspired oxygen tension → Descent; acetazolamide
  10. 72 yo F, POD 2 laparotomy, febrile, SpO2 88%, absent breath sounds at the left base, film shows left lower lobe collapse → Intrapulmonary right-to-left shunt → Incentive spirometry and mobilization
Pearls Normal A-a means hypoventilation or low inspired oxygen; widened and oxygen-responsive means V/Q mismatch; widened and oxygen-refractory means shunt. · Shunt is the hypoxemia that oxygen will not fix. When the FiO2 goes up and the saturation does not follow, stop titrating and start recruiting. Recruit with PEEP (positive end-expiratory pressure), CPAP (continuous positive airway pressure), surfactant, drainage, or a diuretic for the edema behind it. · Hypoventilation is the one hypoxemia with a normal A-a gradient and a high PaCO2; low inspired PO2 is the one with a normal gradient and a low PaCO2 from the compensatory hyperventilation. · A normal PaO2 in a cyanotic patient means the hemoglobin cannot carry oxygen: think of methemoglobin. · Boundary: refractory hypoxemia with clear lungs and no cardiac history can still be an embolus. If it raises right-sided pressures enough to open a PFO (patent foramen ovale), a dead-space disease presents as a right-to-left shunt. Look for the cause of the raised pressure, not just the shunt.
Pairs with Lung Disease in the Newborn and Preterm Infant covers the parenchymal differential by chest film (ground glass and air bronchograms versus retained fluid, meconium, or air leak). Congenital Heart Disease covers the lesions themselves. Cyanosis in the Newborn covers sorting at-rest physiology in the delivery room. This brief covers the mechanism categories above all three. Ask: is the A-a gradient widened, and does the hypoxemia respond to oxygen?
Transferable rule Treat hypoxemia as a physiology question. Compute the A-a gradient, then check what happens on supplemental oxygen. Those two answers name the mechanism before the illness is named.
